props.title: The Way of the Gun
props.initialSlug: Two criminals kidnap a surrogate mother for ransom

sections.content: The Way of the Gun (2000) marks Christopher McQuarrie's directorial debut after his Oscar-winning screenplay for The Usual Suspects (1995). This neo-noir crime thriller channels the brutal efficiency of Point Blank (1967) while anticipating the morally ambiguous violence of No Country for Old Men (2007). McQuarrie crafts a deliberately paced kidnapping story that subverts typical crime film tropes, featuring career criminals who aren't criminal masterminds but desperate men making increasingly poor choices.

sections.content: The film's influence on subsequent crime thrillers is notable, particularly in its unflinching approach to violence and morally compromised characters. Like Heat (1995), it presents professional criminals with a code, but strips away any glamorization. The film's opening scene, a parking lot confrontation that erupts into chaos, sets the tone for McQuarrie's later action work in Mission: Impossible - Rogue Nation (2015) and Fallout (2018) - practical effects, geographic clarity, and consequences for every bullet fired.

Benicio Del Toro and Ryan Phillippe's performances as the amoral protagonists Parker and Longbaugh (named after Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid's real names) draw from the tradition of Reservoir Dogs (1992) and The Getaway (1972), but with a harder edge. James Caan's enforcer Joe Sarno provides the film's moral center, reminiscent of his work in Thief (1981), delivering McQuarrie's sharp dialogue with world-weary authority. sections.content: McQuarrie's approach to action and violence influenced a generation of crime thrillers. The film's DNA can be seen in everything from Drive (2011) to Hell or High Water (2016), where violence erupts suddenly and brutally, stripped of Hollywood glamour. The film's complex plot mechanics and morally ambiguous characters paved the way for neo-noirs like Brick (2005) and Kill List (2011).
